question: Why do massive residual-stream activations and attention sinks co-occur in pre-norm decoder Transformers, what distinct functions do they serve, and which architectural or training interventions can suppress either phenomenon without harming language-model perplexity?

key_findings.claim: Author-reported lifecycle: massive activations are injected abruptly by one or a few early step-up blocks, persist additively through the residual stream, and are cancelled by late step-down blocks.
key_findings.evidence: Across seven listed Llama-2, Llama-3, Qwen2.5, and Qwen3 checkpoints, Table 1 places step-up blocks between indices 4 and 14 and step-down blocks at or near the final blocks. The residual unrolling explains persistence, while block-output traces show late opposite-sign contributions. Appendix figures reproduce the rise-plateau-fall pattern and large quadratic-form norms, although the appendix prose inconsistently calls the displayed set 12 models.

key_findings.claim: Author-reported mechanism: in SwiGLU step-up and step-down FFNs, spike-token gating is approximately linear and selected output coordinates behave as high-gain, nearly rank-one quadratic forms sharing a trigger direction.
key_findings.evidence: The paper rewrites a coordinate as h-tilde^T U_k h-tilde, symmetrizes U_k, and reports that spike channels have anomalously large Frobenius norms and one dominant eigenvalue; principal eigenvectors are said to be nearly common across spike channels. This accounts for synchronized channel spikes when an input aligns with the shared direction. Appendix B derives the quadratic form, but no numeric alignment statistic, spectral-gap table, or uncertainty is supplied.

anchors.section: 3.1.2 Feed-Forward Block as Directional Quadratic Amplifier

key_findings.claim: Contradiction audit: Equation 21 is algebraically inconsistent with the immediately preceding squared-projection approximation.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 20 is lambda-star times (s-star^T h-tilde)^2. Because RMSNorm gives ||h-tilde||_2 = sqrt(d_model), substitution yields lambda-star d_model cos^2(s-star,h-tilde), not the printed lambda-star sqrt(d_model) cos(s-star,h-tilde). The appendix proves the RMS coordinate bound but does not repair this equation. The qualitative alignment story may survive, but the stated scaling and sign dependence do not.

key_findings.claim: Author-reported positional result: almost every vocabulary item becomes a spike token at position zero, so initial-position occupancy rather than token semantics is the dominant trigger in the tested pretrained models.
key_findings.evidence: The vocabulary sweep reports 98.40%-99.93% spike-token ratios for all seven models: 31,887/32,000 for Llama-2-7B through 151,830/151,936 for Qwen3-8B. The proposed explanation is that causal attention for the first token collapses to a prompt-independent linear map that steers its representation toward the FFN trigger direction. The paper does not state the numerical threshold used to classify a vocabulary item as a spike token, limiting reproducibility of the counts.

anchors.section: 3.1.3 What Makes a Token a Spike Token

key_findings.claim: Author interpretation: delimiters become spikes by first self-sinking in early attention blocks and thereby following a stable trajectory into the same FFN trigger manifold.
key_findings.evidence: The text attributes delimiter self-sinking to elevated post-RMSNorm magnitudes and near-collinearity with learned RMSNorm scales, then argues that self-attention makes their transformation resemble the isolated first-token case. Unlike the vocabulary-position sweep, this chain is not accompanied by a delimiter intervention, quantitative collinearity table, or across-model effect size, so it is a plausible mechanism rather than a fully isolated causal result.

key_findings.claim: Author-reported bridge: RMSNorm maps large spike states to bounded, sparse, approximately token-invariant vectors, allowing their keys to occupy a small stable subspace from which sink heads can form.
key_findings.evidence: The paper derives a sqrt(d_model) coordinate bound, argues that a few outlier channels dominate the norm and suppress other coordinates, and shows post-step-up spike-token cosines approaching one in Llama-2-7B. It then proposes that a sink occurs when non-sink queries are closer to this low-dimensional sink-key subspace than to ordinary keys. Figure 6 is a representative t-SNE visualization rather than a quantitative subspace-angle or logit-gap analysis.

key_findings.claim: Author-reported hyperparameter result: sink ratio broadly tracks optimization quality, whereas spike magnitude varies largely independently of both perplexity and sink ratio.
key_findings.evidence: In the scratch-trained 7B ablations, the baseline is perplexity 10.1, sink ratio 46.0%, and spike 3,818. Zero weight decay raises the spike to 12,275 while worsening perplexity to 10.4 and lowering the sink ratio to 33.8%; beta2=0.999 lowers sink ratio to 20.9%. Extending the stated training budget raises sink ratio to 63.3% and lowers perplexity to 9.5 while the spike falls to 1,848. These are single reported runs without uncertainty, and sink ratio is not monotone in perplexity.

key_findings.claim: Contradiction audit: attention-only and single-linear models still develop both phenomena, so the SwiGLU directional amplifier is a mechanism for abrupt, strong spikes in selected pretrained models, not a universal source of massive activations.
key_findings.evidence: Table 4 reports spike/sink values of 688/58.9% for a linear FFN and 637/73.9% for an attention-only model, compared with 3,818/46.0% for SwiGLU and 3,369/69.3% for GeLU. The authors acknowledge that non-gated variants accumulate smaller spikes gradually, which qualifies earlier wording that the SwiGLU FFN is the primary source and the summary's architecture-driven pathway.

key_findings.claim: Author-reported causal decoupling: changing normalization can nearly eliminate spikes while retaining substantial attention sinks and similar C4 perplexity.
key_findings.evidence: Relative to pre-norm (perplexity 10.1, sink 46.0%, spike 3,818), Sandwich Norm gives 9.8/44.7%/520, Sandwich(QK) gives 10.0/42.0%/92, and DynamicTanh gives 10.0/61.0%/153. This is strong negative evidence that large residual spikes are necessary for sinks. However, all three variants still retain pre-block processing or alter more than one normalization pathway; the paper does not train a matched canonical post-norm control, so it does not isolate the abstract's stronger claim that pre-norm itself is the key enabling choice.

key_findings.claim: Author-reported capacity result: per-head dimension is more predictive of sink formation than head count, and concentrating fixed total attention width into fewer larger heads increases sink ratio.
key_findings.evidence: At fixed 32 heads, increasing d_head from 8 to 128 raises sink ratio from 4.1% to 46.0% and improves perplexity from 11.3 to 10.1. With total head capacity fixed, configurations from 8/512 to 256/16 raise sink ratio from 11.0% to 52.1%. Perplexity improves along the same sweep, so the evidence does not disentangle geometric dimension from optimization or model-quality effects.

key_findings.claim: Author-reported substitution result: input-conditioned per-channel or per-head attention gates sharply suppress sinks and spikes, while unconditional and static-signal gates do not.
key_findings.evidence: Conditional channel/head gates yield sink ratios 4.5%/6.4%, spikes 202/186, and perplexities 10.0/10.1. Unconditional variants remain at 41.3%-44.3% sinks, and position- or token-conditioned static signals give 41.1% and 31.1%. The result supports functional substitutability with dynamic routing, but adding gates changes parameters and optimization; it does not prove that an ungated sink head literally computes the same gate.

key_findings.claim: Author-reported context result: removing loss on short positions collapses the sink ratio, consistent with sinks being useful for local prediction under global attention.
key_findings.evidence: With minimum/maximum loss positions 1/4096, the sink ratio is 46.0%; changing to 1024/4096, 1024/5120, 2048/4096, and 2048/6144 gives 13.0%, 8.0%, 1.2%, and 5.8%. Some long-minimum runs instead develop enormous spikes (38,470-42,365). The intervention changes which token positions receive loss and hence the target distribution, not only context length, and no downstream or long-context reasoning metric is reported.

key_findings.claim: Author conclusion: either phenomenon can be suppressed in isolation with no measurable language-model perplexity degradation, arguing against functional necessity of their overlap.
key_findings.evidence: Normalization variants preserve or improve rounded C4 perplexity while suppressing spikes, and conditional gating preserves 10.0-10.1 perplexity while reducing sinks to 4.5%-6.4%. This is meaningful negative evidence for necessity under the tested recipe. It is limited to rounded perplexity from one evaluation corpus without seeds, intervals, quantization, pruning, retrieval, downstream, or long-context tests, so 'without performance cost' is narrower than the paper's efficiency discussion.

key_findings.claim: Contradiction audit: the stated 100B-token baseline budget conflicts by a factor of ten with the appendix's optimization table.
key_findings.evidence: The main experiment and Table 3 label the baseline as 100B training tokens and the extension as 200B. Appendix Table 9 specifies 5,000 training steps and a 2M-token batch, whose product is 10B tokens, absent an unstated multiplier; it also cannot directly explain a 200B run. This materially blocks exact reproduction and calibration of the optimization ablations.

key_findings.claim: Contradiction audit: the appendix alternates between seven and twelve evaluated open-source models even though Table 10 and Figure 7 display seven.
key_findings.evidence: Table 10 enumerates exactly seven checkpoints. The next page says the traces cover 'all 12 evaluated models,' and the Figure 7 caption again says 12, while the displayed panels correspond to the seven listed models. This appears to be a manuscript-count error rather than evidence for five additional architectures.

method.core_idea: Combine mechanistic tracing in pretrained pre-norm Llama/Qwen models with controlled 7B-from-scratch architectural and training ablations, treating spike magnitude and a thresholded head-level sink ratio as separable observables.
method.mechanism: The proposed pathway is: an early FFN (especially SwiGLU/GeLU) amplifies inputs aligned with a shared high-gain quadratic direction; residual addition preserves the resulting few-channel outlier until late cancellation; RMSNorm converts it into a sparse near-constant vector; learned key projections place that vector in a stable low-dimensional subspace; selected heads route ordinary queries toward it as a sink, effectively reducing useful long-range contribution. Dynamic gates can substitute for the routing function, while loss concentrated on later positions reduces the training incentive for it.
assumptions: Llama- and Qwen-family pre-norm decoder models are representative of modern Transformers relevant to the proposed co-occurrence mechanism.
The SiLU gate is close enough to identity on spike tokens for a quadratic approximation to explain the decisive FFN coordinates.
Large Frobenius norms, a dominant eigenvalue, and shared principal directions identify the causal spike amplifier rather than merely correlate with learned spikes.
Residual addition is the main propagation mechanism, and late opposite-sign outputs deliberately neutralize rather than incidentally counterbalance the spikes.
The paper's unstated spike-token and spike-channel thresholds reproduce the reported vocabulary and model comparisons.
A head is meaningfully a sink when, for T=64, some first-half key receives more than epsilon=0.3 average attention; conclusions are assumed robust to these fixed choices despite no sensitivity sweep.
C4 perplexity measured on up to 1024 x 4096 tokens is sufficient to detect meaningful quality loss from suppressing spikes or sinks.
Single-run 7B ablations with rounded perplexity can support causal architecture and training claims without run-to-run uncertainty.
Sandwich Norm, QKNorm, DynamicTanh, and added gating are matched enough to the pre-norm baseline that changes can be attributed to the named mechanism.
Excluding loss on early positions is a valid proxy for changing the training context-length distribution rather than a broader change to supervision and target difficulty.
The intended token budget is the main-text 100B/200B figure despite the appendix's 5,000 x 2M = 10B specification.

techniques.role: Separates post-residual magnitudes from individual block outputs to identify step-up injection, persistence, and step-down cancellation.
Approximates SwiGLU output coordinates as symmetric quadratic forms and inspects their norms, eigenspectra, and trigger directions.
Tests every vocabulary item at the initial position to distinguish positional from semantic spike triggers.
Measures whether RMS-normalized spike representations become sparse and nearly collinear across tokens.
Uses projected key/query geometry and a representative t-SNE view to motivate head-specific sink formation.
Counts heads where a first-half key receives more than 0.3 mean causal attention at sequence length 64.
Compares SwiGLU, GeLU, linear, and attention-only blocks to test whether gated FFNs are necessary.
Uses Sandwich Norm, QKNorm, and DynamicTanh to suppress residual spikes while observing retained sinks.
Varies head count, head dimension, and fixed-total-width factorizations to test the subspace-capacity hypothesis.
Contrasts hidden-state-conditioned, unconditional, positional, and token-embedding gates as substitutes for sink routing.
Removes short-position prediction losses to test whether local-dependence training induces sinks.
Cross-checks formulas, model counts, sink definitions, and training-token arithmetic against main-text claims.

evaluations.setting: Seven pretrained Llama-2/3 and Qwen2.5/3 checkpoints from 7B to 14B, tracing top-three post-residual and block-output coordinates over depth (pp. 3-4).
evaluations.metric: Step-up/step-down block indices, maximal coordinate trajectories, quadratic-form Frobenius norms, and qualitative eigenspectra.
evaluations.result: Every listed model shows early injection (block 4-14), a long intermediate plateau, and cancellation at or near its final blocks; high-norm U_k coordinates align with spike channels (p. 4), with appendix plots extending the observation (pp. 19-21).
evaluations.baseline: Ordinary channels and blocks outside the identified step-up/step-down locations.

evaluations.setting: Every vocabulary item placed at position zero in each of the seven pretrained checkpoints (pp. 5-6).
evaluations.metric: Count and fraction classified as spike tokens.
evaluations.result: The reported fractions range from 98.40% for Qwen2.5 to 99.93% for Qwen3, with Llama models at 99.65%-99.77%; the classification threshold is not defined (p. 6).
evaluations.baseline: The same token identities at later positions, described as rarely spiking but not tabulated.

evaluations.setting: Llama-style 7B scratch pretraining on DCLM with learning-rate, minimum-LR, weight-decay, beta2, and stated token-budget variations; C4 evaluation (p. 8).
evaluations.metric: Perplexity, epsilon=0.3/T=64 sink ratio, and maximum spike magnitude.
evaluations.result: The baseline is 10.1 perplexity, 46.0% sinks, and spike 3,818; zero weight decay gives 10.4/33.8%/12,275, beta2=0.999 gives 10.7/20.9%/1,855, and the stated 200B run gives 9.5/63.3%/1,848 (p. 8).
evaluations.baseline: Nominal 100B-token, 3e-4 learning-rate, beta2=0.95, weight-decay=0.1 recipe, whose appendix arithmetic instead totals 10B tokens.

evaluations.setting: Matched 7B models replacing the feed-forward block with GeLU, one linear layer, or another attention layer (pp. 8-9).
evaluations.metric: C4 perplexity, sink ratio, and maximum spike.
evaluations.result: GeLU gives 10.1/69.3%/3,369, linear 12.5/58.9%/688, attention-only 10.8/73.9%/637, and SwiGLU 10.1/46.0%/3,818; both phenomena survive every design (pp. 8-9).

evaluations.setting: Matched normalization variants: Sandwich Norm, Sandwich(QK), DynamicTanh, and standard pre-norm (p. 9).
evaluations.metric: C4 perplexity, sink ratio, and maximum spike.
evaluations.result: Sandwich, Sandwich(QK), and DynamicTanh reduce spikes from 3,818 to 520, 92, and 153 while retaining sink ratios 44.7%, 42.0%, and 61.0% and perplexities 9.8-10.0 (p. 9).
evaluations.baseline: Pre-norm at 10.1 perplexity, 46.0% sinks, and spike 3,818.

evaluations.setting: Head-count, head-dimension, and constant-total-attention-width sweeps in scratch-trained 7B models (pp. 9-10).
evaluations.metric: C4 perplexity, sink ratio, and maximum spike.
evaluations.result: At fixed 32 heads, d_head 8 to 128 raises sinks 4.1% to 46.0%; at fixed total width, moving from 8/512 to 256/16 raises sinks 11.0% to 52.1%, with simultaneous perplexity improvement (p. 10).

evaluations.setting: Conditional per-channel/head/token gates, unconditional gates, and gates conditioned on static position or token embedding (p. 10).
evaluations.metric: C4 perplexity, sink ratio, and maximum spike.
evaluations.result: Conditional channel/head gates reach 4.5%/6.4% sinks and spikes 202/186 at 10.0/10.1 perplexity; unconditional and positional gates remain above 41% sinks, while token-embedding gating leaves 31.1% (p. 10).
evaluations.baseline: Ungated pre-norm baseline with 46.0% sinks, spike 3,818, and perplexity 10.1.

evaluations.setting: Loss-position ranges with minimum/maximum positions 1/256 through 2048/6144, presented as context-length training ablations (pp. 10-11).
evaluations.metric: C4 perplexity, sink ratio, and maximum spike.
evaluations.result: Keeping minimum position 1 leaves 42.1%-46.3% sinks, while minimum 1024 gives 8.0%-13.0% and minimum 2048 gives 1.2%-5.8%; several long-minimum variants show spikes 30,634-42,365 (p. 10).
evaluations.baseline: Loss over positions 1-4096 at 10.1 perplexity, 46.0% sinks, and spike 3,818.

limitations: [Author-stated] The detailed directional-amplifier instantiation is developed primarily for Llama-2-7B; other models are said to share the high-level mechanism but differ in details (p. 4).
[Author-stated] The work evaluates language modeling rather than directly demonstrating quantization, pruning, KV-cache, or long-context efficiency improvements discussed as motivation (pp. 1, 12).

[Reviewer-inferred] The scratch ablations use one 7B Llama-style recipe and report no seed count, confidence interval, significance test, or run variance; many conclusions rest on rounded 0.1 perplexity differences (pp. 8-10, 17).
[Reviewer-inferred] The main text states 100B baseline tokens, but Appendix A's 5,000 steps x 2M tokens totals 10B unless an unstated multiplier exists (pp. 8, 17).
[Reviewer-inferred] No operational magnitude threshold for spike tokens or channels is supplied, despite exact vocabulary-wide spike counts and categorical references throughout (pp. 3, 5-6).

[Reviewer-inferred] Sink ratio uses only epsilon=0.3 and T=64 and asks whether any first-half position crosses the threshold; there is no threshold, length, positional, or corpus sensitivity analysis (p. 17).

[Reviewer-inferred] The geometric sink account relies on a representative t-SNE plot and qualitative subspace language, without principal angles, intrinsic-dimension estimates, logit-gap distributions, or interventions along the claimed subspaces (p. 7).
[Reviewer-inferred] The shared trigger direction, rank-one dominance, and near-identity SiLU claims lack across-model numeric summaries or uncertainty; Appendix C mainly adds plots (pp. 4-5, 20-21).

[Reviewer-inferred] The normalization study lacks a canonical matched post-norm model, so it shows that several alternative normalization paths decouple spikes and sinks but does not isolate pre-norm as the unique enabling choice (p. 9).
[Reviewer-inferred] Gating variants add parameters and change optimization, with no parameter-matched inactive-gate control; functional substitutability is not identity of mechanism (p. 10).
[Reviewer-inferred] The context intervention removes supervision at early token positions and changes target/data distributions, so it does not solely manipulate usable context length (pp. 10-11).

[Reviewer-inferred] Suppression quality is tested only with C4 perplexity; no downstream, calibration, robustness, retrieval, generation-length, or quantized-serving metrics establish the broader 'no performance cost' implication (pp. 9-12, 17).
[Reviewer-inferred] Equation 21 drops a square and a factor of sqrt(d_model), making the stated amplifier scaling incorrect (p. 5).
[Reviewer-inferred] Table 10 lists seven models while the following prose and Figure 7 caption claim twelve, leaving the claimed evaluation breadth internally inconsistent (pp. 19-20).
failure_modes: A spike detector built from this paper cannot be reproduced exactly because the classification threshold is absent.
The fixed epsilon=0.3/T=64 sink ratio can label threshold crossings as architectural changes even when attention redistribution is small or moves beyond the first half.
A large spike may saturate the normalized sparse direction without increasing sink behavior, so spike magnitude is a poor proxy for functional influence.
Attention-only and linear models can accumulate spikes through a different pathway; interventions aimed only at SwiGLU quadratic directions will miss those cases.
Sandwich or element-wise normalization can remove spikes while the model learns an alternative sink representation, so spike suppression alone does not guarantee sink or KV-cache mitigation.
Dynamic gates can replace sink routing in perplexity while changing downstream head specialization, robustness, or calibration in unmeasured ways.
Removing short-position losses may suppress sinks by changing supervision rather than by teaching genuinely better long-range use, and can produce even larger residual spikes.
Perplexity parity can conceal harms to rare tokens, long contexts, factual recall, generation stability, or low-precision deployment.
Equation 21's incorrect scaling can mislead attempts to predict spike magnitude from cosine alignment or model width.
The 10B-versus-100B discrepancy can cause replicas to compare models at substantially different optimization stages, which itself changes sink ratio.
Qualitative t-SNE separation can be projection-dependent and need not reflect causal high-dimensional key-query distances.
Conclusions from Llama/Qwen pre-norm dense decoders may fail for mixture-of-experts, post-norm, normalization-free, recurrent, state-space, multimodal, or encoder architectures.
reusable_insights: Trace an outlier in block outputs and the post-residual stream separately; injection, propagation, and cancellation are distinct mechanisms.
For gated MLPs, factor an extreme output coordinate into a symmetric quadratic form and inspect spectrum and input alignment rather than only weight magnitudes.
Test positional hypotheses by sweeping token identity at fixed position and position at fixed identity; always publish the classification threshold.
Do not infer functional coupling from co-location: seek interventions that preserve A while removing B and vice versa.
When a normalized outlier becomes approximately constant, analyze it as an input-dependent implicit parameter but verify causality by subtracting or replacing that fixed direction.
Separate per-head dimension from total attention width; factorization can matter even at fixed parameter capacity.
Compare dynamic, unconditional, and static-signal gates to identify whether routing depends on the evolving representation.
Treat the positions receiving training loss as part of the data distribution, not merely as a context-length hyperparameter.
Pair thresholded sink ratios with continuous received-attention, logit-gap, value-output, and downstream contribution metrics.
Cross-check token arithmetic, equation dimensions, and enumerated model counts before interpreting a mechanistic ablation suite.
open_questions: What exact activation threshold reproduces the reported spike-token counts, and are results stable across percentile-, scale-, and model-normalized definitions?
Does a canonical post-norm model, matched in compute and quality, suppress spikes while retaining sinks, directly supporting the claimed pre-norm causality?
Do principal-angle and causal subspace interventions confirm the proposed sink-key/query geometry across heads, prompts, layers, and model families?
Does replacing the learned near-constant spike direction with an explicit bias preserve behavior, establishing the 'implicit parameter' interpretation causally?
Do matched-parameter dynamic gates reproduce local routing while preserving downstream, calibration, robustness, and long-context behavior?
How do conclusions vary with sink threshold, evaluation length, sequence position, corpus, and value-weighted attention contribution?
Is the intended scratch-training budget 10B, 100B, or another effective token count, and do replicas recover every table at the corrected budget?
Why do long-minimum-loss models sometimes produce 30k-42k spikes even while sinks collapse, and what function do those spikes serve?
Can the amplifier theory be generalized to the attention-only and linear models that still form massive activations?
Do independent suppressions improve actual FP4/INT4 quantization, pruning, KV-cache compression, throughput, and long-context retrieval?
How do MoE, multimodal, encoder, normalization-free, post-norm, and hybrid attention/state-space architectures alter the lifecycle?
Can longitudinal training checkpoints distinguish whether optimization health causes sink formation or both merely track training progress?

competitive_landscape.title: Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks
competitive_landscape.difference: StreamingLLM introduced the attention-sink phenomenon as strong, often nonsemantic attention to initial tokens and exploited preserved sink KVs for stable streaming to millions of tokens. The target does not introduce sinks or their deployment utility; it studies their training/architectural relation to massive activations and proposes a local-routing account.

competitive_landscape.title: Massive Activations in Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Sun et al. established massive activations, near input-invariance, implicit-bias behavior, and their concentration of attention on corresponding tokens. The target extends this line with step-up/step-down FFN factorization and decoupling ablations, but its global implicit-parameter and spike-to-sink framing substantially builds on this predecessor.

competitive_landscape.title: When Attention Sink Emerges in Language Models: An Empirical View
competitive_landscape.difference: Gu et al. already traced sink emergence during pretraining across optimization, data, loss, and architecture, interpreted sinks as largely noninformative key biases, and suppressed them with unnormalized sigmoid attention up to 1B. The target adds 7B ablations, massive-activation coupling, head-dimension and loss-position results, and a dynamic-routing interpretation.

competitive_landscape.title: Active-Dormant Attention Heads: Mechanistically Demystifying Extreme-Token Phenomena in LLMs
competitive_landscape.difference: Guo et al. jointly analyze attention sinks, value drains, and residual peaks through an active-dormant head mechanism, prove mutual-reinforcement dynamics in a toy task, and test ReLU attention/SGD mitigations in pretrained LLMs. The target instead emphasizes pre-norm residual/FFN geometry, independent suppression, explicit gate substitution, and short-position supervision in a larger scratch recipe.

competitive_landscape.title: A Refined Analysis of Massive Activations in LLMs
competitive_landscape.difference: Owen et al. already show across GLU and non-GLU architectures that suppressing massive activations need not collapse perplexity or downstream performance, and combine TVR with KV bias or DynamicTanh. The target's spike-not-necessary result is therefore confirmatory; its distinctive extension is retained sink measurement and a proposed architectural bridge/local-routing split.

competitive_landscape.title: Attention Sinks and Compression Valleys in LLMs are Two Sides of the Same Coin
competitive_landscape.difference: Queipo-de-Llano et al. already connect massive residual activations to attention sinks and representational compression, provide entropy bounds, validate models from 410M to 120B, and propose a Mix-Compress-Refine depth theory. The target focuses on why co-occurrence is contingent rather than necessary and contributes controlled normalization, gate, head-dimension, and context-position ablations, but it does not establish the first unified view.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim to move beyond descriptive co-occurrence by giving a mechanistic account in which pre-norm connects global implicit-parameter spikes to local sink routing, showing head dimension and short-context training drive sinks, and independently suppressing either phenomenon without language-model degradation.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper contributes a coordinated suite of pretrained tracing and 7B scratch ablations: residual lifecycle, quadratic FFN spectra, full-vocabulary position-zero probes, normalization decoupling, head-capacity factorization, conditional gate substitution, and loss-position controls (pp. 3-11), with derivations and additional plots in Appendices A-C (pp. 17-21).
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The strongest defensible novelty is the integrated ablation suite and the specific directional-amplifier plus dynamic-local-routing hypothesis. Massive activations, sink co-location, implicit-bias interpretations, unified extreme-token mechanisms, training/architecture dependence, DynamicTanh mitigation, and even a prior joint activation-sink-compression theory are all version-pinned predecessors. Claims that pre-norm is the key causal choice and that sinks are literally implicit gates remain suggestive because there is no canonical post-norm control or matched gate-equivalence test; confidence is further reduced by the token-budget, equation, and model-count inconsistencies.

reviewer_notes: Read the complete 21-page extracted primary PDF, including all tables, references, Appendix A hyperparameters and sink definition, Appendix B derivations, and Appendix C model/figure extensions. Findings explicitly separate author reports from reviewer inference and contradiction audits. The source corresponds to arXiv v1 submitted 2026-03-05; literature was checked against version-pinned primary arXiv records current through 2026-08-23. Residual concerns are the absent spike threshold, lack of seeds and metric sensitivities, qualitative geometry, no canonical post-norm control, the 100B-versus-10B arithmetic conflict, Equation 21 error, and seven-versus-twelve model-count error.
